positions.claim: Giving an agent the user's own credentials or personal token is the wrong model; agents should receive delegated authority scoped to specific actions instead.
OAuth-style scopes such as 'read' are too coarse for agents, and fine-grained capabilities should replace them.
Even fine-grained OAuth is insufficient because it still mints a token for the user; the agent must be the principal that holds the token.
Every agent should hold its own private key and sign its own tokens so actions are attributable per agent, per host, and per user.
Agents are never fully detached principals — each one always reports to a user.
Read-type capabilities should be granted by default per host because prompting for approval on every action would make the system unusable.
A proxy architecture for agent authorization is a bad idea because handling the data makes it unscalable; a directory that matches intent to capabilities is the right shape.
AI gateways do not provide per-agent identity or lifecycle traceability, which is what distinguishes this protocol from them.
Because few or no services implement agent-native auth endpoints today, translating existing OpenAPI specs into capabilities is a necessary interim bridge.
The v1 spec's assumption that agents are ephemeral is outdated, and long-lived and organizational agents require policy support being added in v2.
Agent security should not be an enterprise-only concern; the protocol is open source so that individual AI users benefit too.
